title: Muktinath pilgrimage by air via Jomsom
meta_description: Muktinath pilgrimage by air, 4 nights from Kathmandu: fly to Jomsom, shraddha at Kagbeni, a night beside the temple and dawn bath under the 108 spouts.
summary: A four-night pilgrimage from Kathmandu to Muktinath, flying to Jomsom to avoid the long road, with a night at Kagbeni for shraddha rites at the confluence and a night at Ranipauwa so you can bathe under the 108 spouts at dawn. Gentle pace, sensible acclimatisation, a guide who knows the rituals.
intro: For Hindus, Muktinath is Mukti Kshetra, the place of liberation, and one of the 108 Divya Desam shrines of Vishnu praised by the Tamil Alvar poets. For Buddhists it is Chumig Gyatsa, the Hundred Springs, where Guru Rinpoche is said to have meditated on his way to Tibet. Both come to the same small walled compound at about 3,710 m, and both leave with water from its springs. Few pilgrimages in Nepal reach this height so easily.

Many pilgrims rush the journey, flying from Pokhara to Jomsom and driving straight up to the temple in a morning, and some of them feel the altitude badly. We go a little slower: a night at Kagbeni first, where many families offer pinda for their ancestors at the river, then a night at Ranipauwa below the temple so your darshan is at dawn, before the crowds and the wind. The whole journey takes five days from Kathmandu.
story: The plane climbs out of Pokhara's green bowl and into a gorge so deep that Dhaulagiri and Annapurna stand on either wingtip. At Jomsom the air is thin and dry and smells of dust and juniper. Kagbeni greets you with prayer wheels and the roar of two rivers meeting, where a priest helps you offer rice balls to those who came before you. Next day the road climbs past Jharkot's old fort to Ranipauwa, the queen's rest house that gave the pilgrim village its name. At first light you walk up through the poplars to the temple, where water pours from 108 bronze spouts and a small flame burns beside a spring, and you understand why people have walked here for so long.
highlights: Darshan at Muktinath at dawn, with time for the 108 spouts and the two kunds
Jwala Mai, where a natural gas flame burns beside a spring, honoured by Hindus and Buddhists alike
Shraddha or pinda rites at the Kagbeni confluence with a local priest
Searching the Kali Gandaki for Shaligram stones, the fossil ammonites worshipped as Vishnu
A short, gentle schedule with flights in both directions

days.title: Kathmandu to Pokhara
days.text: We fly from Kathmandu to Pokhara and check into a hotel near Phewa Lake. Your guide, who has accompanied many pilgrim families, explains the rituals at Kagbeni and Muktinath and what to bring: a change of clothes and a towel for the bath, a small container for holy water, and offerings if you wish. In the evening you can take a boat to the Tal Barahi temple on the lake. Early night, as the Jomsom flight leaves at first light.

days.title: Fly to Jomsom, drive to Kagbeni
days.text: The short flight lands in Jomsom before the wind rises. We drive up the riverbed to Kagbeni, where the Jhong and Kali Gandaki rivers meet. Rest after lunch to let your body adjust. In the afternoon a local priest can lead shraddha or pinda rites for your ancestors at the confluence, which many families consider especially meritorious here. Walk the village's covered lanes and visit Kag Chode monastery. Our guide will also show you how to look for Shaligram stones on the riverbed.

days.title: Kagbeni to Muktinath
days.text: We drive up the Jhong valley past Jharkot to Ranipauwa, the pilgrim village below the temple, and check into a lodge. After lunch and a rest, walk slowly up to the compound, or ride a pony. See the main temple of Shri Muktinarayan, the 108 water spouts in a semicircle behind it, and Jwala Mai, where a flame of natural gas burns beside a spring. Evening prayers and lamps in the Buddhist shrines make a quiet end to the day.

days.title: Dawn bath and down to Jomsom
days.text: We walk up at first light. Pilgrims bathe under the 108 spouts, running along the line in icy water, then dip in the two kunds in front of the temple, believed to wash away the weight of past deeds. Then darshan of Vishnu, offerings and blessings. Our guide keeps your belongings dry and warm clothes ready. After breakfast we drive down to Jomsom, warmer and lower, for a rest and a final evening with apple pie and tea.

days.title: Fly to Pokhara and Kathmandu
days.text: The morning flight takes you to Pokhara, and we connect to Kathmandu the same day where flights allow. The pilgrimage ends on arrival. If the Jomsom flight is cancelled by wind or cloud, we either wait for the next morning or drive to Pokhara by jeep, about 8 to 10 hours, so please keep a spare day before onward travel. We can also arrange a night in Pokhara on the way back if you prefer a gentler finish.

includes: Licensed guide experienced with pilgrim groups
One night in Pokhara with breakfast and three nights in lodges with all meals, vegetarian on request
Jeep transfers in Mustang and airport transfers
excludes: Priest's dakshina and puja materials at Kagbeni and Muktinath
good_to_know: Indian citizens do not need a visa for Nepal but should carry a passport or voter ID; the conservation area permit for SAARC nationals is NPR 1,000. Check current status before you travel.
Since April 2023 foreign visitors to conservation areas are expected to travel with a licensed guide; check current status before you travel.
Jomsom flights fly only in the morning and are often delayed or cancelled; keep at least one spare day.
The temple is at about 3,710 m; people with heart or lung conditions should consult a doctor before travelling.
Lodges at Ranipauwa are simple and fill up with pilgrim groups in spring and autumn; we book ahead and request rooms close to the temple path.

faqs.q: How do I reach Muktinath from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: The quickest way is to fly from Kathmandu to Pokhara (25 minutes), then from Pokhara to Jomsom (20 minutes), then drive about 1.5 hours to Muktinath. You can also drive the whole way, around 380 km over two long days. Helicopter day trips from Pokhara or Kathmandu exist but give very little time at altitude to adjust or pray.

faqs.q: What is the significance of the 108 water spouts at Muktinath?
faqs.a: Behind the main Vishnu temple, 108 spouts shaped like bull heads pour water from the springs above. Hindus believe bathing under all 108 cleanses past sins and brings mukti, or liberation. The number 108 is sacred in both Hinduism and Buddhism. Pilgrims run along the line of spouts in icy water, then dip in the two kunds in front of the temple.

faqs.q: Why is Muktinath sacred to Buddhists?
faqs.a: Tibetan Buddhists call Muktinath Chumig Gyatsa, the Hundred Springs, and believe Guru Rinpoche, Padmasambhava, meditated here on his way to Tibet. The compound includes Buddhist shrines, and the Jwala Mai flame, burning from natural gas beside a spring, is honoured by both faiths as a meeting of earth, water and fire. Buddhist nuns help tend the temple.

faqs.q: Is one night enough at Muktinath?
faqs.a: One night at Ranipauwa is enough for most pilgrims and lets you visit the temple twice, in the afternoon and at dawn. Staying overnight also means you are not rushing up and down in one day at 3,700 m, which is when altitude problems usually appear. If you want time for longer pujas or to rest, add a second night.

Yes, many elderly pilgrims make the journey every year. Flying in and sleeping at Kagbeni first makes it easier. From Ranipauwa to the temple is a slow 15 to 20 minute walk uphill, and ponies or porters can carry those who cannot walk. A doctor's check before you travel is wise, especially for heart, lung or blood pressure conditions.

Shaligrams are black fossil ammonites, sea creatures some 150 million years old, found in the bed of the Kali Gandaki around Kagbeni and further north. Hindus worship them as natural forms of Vishnu and keep them in household shrines. Our guide can show you where to look on the riverbed. Small pieces are also sold in Jomsom and Ranipauwa.

faqs.q: Can I perform shraddha at Kagbeni?
faqs.a: Yes. Kagbeni, at the confluence of the Kali Gandaki and Jhong rivers, is considered a sacred place for shraddha and pinda daan, offerings to ancestors. Local priests perform the rites by the river, usually in the morning or afternoon. Tell us in advance and we will arrange a priest and materials. Dakshina is given directly to the priest.

faqs.q: What is the best time for the Muktinath yatra?
faqs.a: March to May and September to November are best, with clear skies and reliable flights. Winter, December to February, is very cold and Muktinath may have snow, but the temple stays open and crowds are thin. The monsoon months are hardest, with flight cancellations and landslides on the road below Jomsom.

faqs.q: What should I wear and carry for the temple bath?
faqs.a: Bring a full change of clothes, a quick-dry towel, warm layers and a hat. The water from the spouts is close to freezing, and the wind can be strong by late morning, so bathe early. Carry a small bottle for holy water, and leave valuables with your guide. Shoes come off inside the temple area.
